title: A HIGH PRIEST WAS FORBIDDEN TO MARRY A WOMAN WITH A PAST—BUT THE REASON WILL LEAD YOU STRAIGHT TO JESUS
paragraphs: A HIGH PRIEST WAS FORBIDDEN TO MARRY A WOMAN WITH A PAST—BUT THE REASON WILL LEAD YOU STRAIGHT TO JESUS

The shocking marriage command in Leviticus 21:13–15, the holiness of God's priesthood, and the breathtaking Gospel truth that the Bride of Christ is made pure not because she never sinned, but because Jesus gave Himself to cleanse her.
There is something unsettling about a Bible verse that seems to say a woman with a painful past could never become the wife of Israel's high priest.
Not a widow.
Not a divorced woman.
Not even a woman whose sexual history placed her outside the specific requirements of the priestly marriage law.
The high priest was commanded to marry a virgin from his own people.
And perhaps your first reaction is the same question that has troubled many readers.
Why would God give such a command?
Was He saying that a widow was worth less? That a divorced woman could never be honorable? That a woman who had sinned was permanently disqualified from being loved?
And if that were the message, what hope would there be for the woman who regrets her past?
What about the man whose private sins still haunt him?
What about the believer who has been forgiven by God but still struggles to forgive himself?
Before we answer, there is something you need to know.
The same Bible that commanded Israel's high priest to marry a virgin also reveals a greater High Priest who gave His life to make sinners clean.
And when you understand the difference between those two realities, a passage that first appears to be about exclusion begins pointing toward the astonishing mercy of Jesus Christ.
But we must not rush past what the Scripture actually says.
Because the truth is more beautiful when we refuse to twist it.
Leviticus 21:13–15 declares:

"And he shall take a wife in her virginity. A widow, or a divorced woman, or profane, or an harlot, these shall he not take: but he shall take a virgin of his own people to wife. Neither shall he profane his seed among his people: for I the LORD do sanctify him."
— Leviticus 21:13–15, KJV
Notice something immediately.
This was not a universal marriage command given to every Israelite man.
It was a special requirement for the high priest, the man occupying the highest office within Israel's priesthood.
And that distinction changes everything.
The high priest was not merely a religious leader with an impressive title. He held an extraordinary responsibility under the covenant God established with Israel.
He represented the people in sacred priestly service.
He carried out duties associated with the sanctuary.
And once a year, on the Day of Atonement, he entered the Most Holy Place with sacrificial blood, following the commands God had given through Moses.
Leviticus 16 describes the solemnity of that day.
The high priest could not approach God's holy presence casually.
He could not invent his own way of worship.
He could not substitute personal preference for divine instruction.
Even his garments, conduct, and family responsibilities were regulated by the holiness of the office he carried.
And that is where the marriage command belongs.
Not in a conversation about whether certain women were less human.
Not in a declaration that everyone with a complicated past was beyond redemption.
But in the sacred context of a priestly office that God had set apart.
The Hebrew text makes this especially clear.
Leviticus 21:13 begins:
וְהוּא אִשָּׁה בִבְתוּלֶיהָ יִקָּח
Vehu ishah vivtuleha yiqqach.
A close translation is:
"And he shall take a wife in her virginity."
The Hebrew word בְּתוּלֶיהָ (betuleha) refers to her virginity, and the command specifically concerns the woman whom the high priest was permitted to marry.
Then verse 15 gives the reason in language that deserves careful attention:
וְלֹא־יְחַלֵּל זַרְעוֹ בְּעַמָּיו כִּי אֲנִי יְהוָה מְקַדְּשׁוֹ
Velo-yechallel zar'o be'ammav, ki ani Adonai meqaddesho.
A close translation is:
"And he shall not profane his offspring among his people, for I am the LORD who sanctifies him."
The word יְחַלֵּל (yechallel) carries the idea of profaning or treating as common something that belongs within a holy order.
And מְקַדְּשׁוֹ (meqaddesho) means "the One who sanctifies him" or "the One who sets him apart."
That final statement is crucial.
God was not explaining the command by saying that every widow or divorced woman was morally corrupt.
He was grounding the command in the consecration of the high priest.
"For I am the LORD who sanctifies him."
The high priest's marriage and descendants were matters of covenantal and priestly significance.
The law protected the distinctiveness of his sacred office and the household connected with it.
That is the reason the passage itself gives.
We should also be careful not to invent additional reasons and then present them as if Moses wrote them.

The text does not explicitly say that the requirement existed because widows were spiritually contaminated, because every divorced woman had committed sexual sin, or because a virgin possessed greater human worth.
Those conclusions go beyond Scripture.
In fact, other passages prevent us from making them.
Leviticus 21:7 gives marriage restrictions for ordinary priests, while Ezekiel 44:22 describes circumstances in which priests could marry widows of priests.
The high priest's requirements were more restrictive because of his particular office.
And throughout the Old Testament, God repeatedly commands His people to protect widows rather than despise them.
Deuteronomy 10:18 declares that God executes justice for the fatherless and widow.
Psalm 68:5 describes Him as a defender of widows.
And the book of Ruth tells a story that should make anyone hesitate before treating widowhood as a mark of spiritual inferiority.
Ruth was a widow.
She was also a Moabite woman who entered Israel's covenant community.
And God, in His providence, brought her into the family line that would eventually lead to David—and ultimately to Jesus Christ.
Think about that.
The God who gave a particular marriage restriction to Israel's high priest also chose to include a faithful widow in the ancestry of the Messiah.
The law distinguished a sacred office. It did not erase the dignity of women who could not marry its holder.
And there is another important distinction.
Virginity, in the ancient priestly marriage command, was a literal marital requirement.
It was not a measurement of how much God loved a woman.
Nor was it a guarantee that someone possessed a sinless heart.
A person can meet an outward requirement and still need forgiveness.
And a person can have a painful past and yet become a remarkable example of faith.
That is not an excuse to dismiss God's standards for sexual holiness.
It is a reminder that holiness must never be reduced to a single outward condition.
Because God sees the heart.
And the heart is where every one of us eventually stands exposed.
Perhaps that is why this passage can become so personal.
You may not be reading it as a scholar trying to understand ancient Israel.
You may be reading it as someone who has made mistakes.
Someone who once trusted the wrong person.
Someone who crossed boundaries you now wish you had respected.
Someone who experienced betrayal, abandonment, or divorce.
Someone whose marriage ended despite years of prayers.
Or someone who has never been married but carries secret shame that no one at church knows about.
You read the words "he shall take a virgin," and something inside you whispers:
Then what about someone like me?
Listen carefully.
Leviticus 21:13–15 was never written to announce that your past makes you permanently unworthy of God's mercy.
And we know this because the Bible does not end in Leviticus.
It leads us to Christ.
But before we arrive at the cross, we need to understand why Israel needed a priesthood in the first place.
The priesthood existed within a system of worship that continually confronted Israel with the holiness of God and the seriousness of sin.
Sin was not a minor inconvenience.
It was rebellion against the God who created us.
It corrupted relationships.
It defiled worship.
It brought guilt and death.
And the sacrificial system taught Israel that reconciliation with God could not be treated lightly.
Yet there was a problem.
Even the high priest was a sinner.
The man who represented the people before God needed atonement himself.
Leviticus 16:6 required Aaron to offer a sin offering for himself and his household.
Imagine the weight of that reality.
The high priest could wear sacred garments.
He could fulfill the prescribed marriage requirements.
He could descend from the appointed priestly family.
He could enter the sanctuary according to God's commands.
And still, he could not claim to be without sin.
The office was holy.
The man was not morally perfect.
That tension was never going to be resolved by finding a better human priest.
It required someone greater.
Someone who would not merely offer sacrifices.
Someone who would become the sacrifice.
Someone who would not merely enter an earthly sanctuary.
Someone who would open the way into God's presence.
And this is where the Gospel begins to shine.
Hebrews 4:14 identifies Jesus as our great High Priest.
Hebrews 4:15 tells us that He was tempted as we are, yet without sin.
Hebrews 7:26 describes Him as holy, harmless, undefiled, and separate from sinners.
Hebrews 7:27 explains that, unlike the former high priests, Jesus did not need to offer sacrifices for His own sins.
He had none.
He offered Himself once for all.
And Hebrews 9:12 declares:
"Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us."
— Hebrews 9:12, KJV
Do you see the difference?
The priests of Israel served under a system that pointed beyond itself.
Jesus fulfilled the priestly mission in a way no ordinary descendant of Aaron could accomplish.
And Hebrews is careful to explain that Christ's priesthood is according to the order of Melchizedek, not a continuation of the Aaronic priesthood in every legal detail.
That matters.
Because we must not carelessly transfer every marriage regulation from Leviticus onto Jesus as if He were an Aaronic high priest seeking a literal wife.
The New Testament does something far richer.
It presents Jesus as the great High Priest.
And it also presents Him as the Bridegroom.
These are distinct biblical images that together reveal different dimensions of His saving work.
Jesus is the High Priest who intercedes for His people.
Jesus is the Bridegroom who loves His Church.
And the Church is described as His bride.
Now the story takes a turn that should leave every repentant sinner overwhelmed by grace.
Because when Scripture describes Christ's bride, it does not pretend that the people who belong to Him have always lived pure lives.
Far from it.
The Church is made up of people rescued from sin.
People who once worshiped idols.
People who lied.
People who lusted.
People who hated.
People who were proud.
People who compromised.
People who were enslaved to destructive desires.
People who desperately needed a Savior.
Paul reminds the Corinthians of their former lives, then announces:
"And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God."
— 1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV
"And such were some of you."
Not "such must you remain forever."
Not "your past has the final word."
Not "your worst sin is your permanent identity."
But "such were some of you."
And then comes the miracle.
"You are washed."
"You are sanctified."
"You are justified."
Not because the past never happened.
Not because sin was harmless.
Not because God lowered His standard.
But because Jesus Christ is powerful enough to forgive sinners and transform their lives.
The Greek text of 1 Corinthians 6:11 includes the words:
ἀπελούσασθε, ἡγιάσθητε, ἐδικαιώθητε
Apelousasthe, hēgiasthēte, edikaiōthēte.
"You were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified."
Paul is describing a decisive change in the believers' standing and identity through Christ and the Spirit.
This is not self-improvement dressed in religious language.
This is salvation.
And if you have ever wondered whether God can do something holy with a life that has been deeply stained, you need to hear what Paul says next about the Church.
Ephesians 5:25–27 declares:

"Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it; That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word, That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish."
— Ephesians 5:25–27, KJV
Read that again.
Christ loved the Church.
Christ gave Himself for the Church.
Christ sanctifies and cleanses the Church.
Christ will present the Church in holiness.
The beauty of Christ's bride is not that she never needed cleansing. It is that her Bridegroom loved her enough to give Himself for her cleansing.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain in sin.
Not an excuse to celebrate rebellion.
Not a declaration that repentance is unnecessary.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace brings sinners out of darkness.
The blood of Jesus does not make sin acceptable.
It makes forgiveness possible.
And the Holy Spirit begins transforming those who belong to Christ.
The Greek word used for "sanctify" in Ephesians 5:26 is ἁγιάσῃ (hagiasē), from a verb meaning to make holy or set apart.
This is the work Christ accomplishes for His people.
He does not merely announce that His bride is acceptable while leaving her unchanged.
He cleanses her.
He sanctifies her.
He prepares her.
And He will complete what He has begun.
That is why the New Testament can speak of the Church's purity without pretending that every Christian has lived an untouched life.
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 11:2:
The Greek phrase is:
παρθένον ἁγνὴν τῷ Χριστῷ
Parthenon hagnēn tō Christō.
"A pure virgin to Christ."
Here Paul is using the imagery of betrothal and purity to express the Church's exclusive faithfulness to Christ.
It is not a statement that every Christian has remained physically unmarried or sexually inexperienced.
It is a call to undivided devotion to the Lord.
And that distinction is essential.
Leviticus speaks of a literal requirement for the high priest's wife.
Paul uses bridal imagery to speak of the Church's spiritual faithfulness.
The passages are not identical laws.
But together, within the larger biblical story, they help us appreciate how seriously God regards holiness—and how wonderfully Christ makes His people holy.
Now imagine something.
Imagine standing before the Lord with every hidden sin exposed.
Not just the mistakes other people know about.
The thoughts you never admitted.
The envy you disguised.
The bitterness you justified.
The lust you entertained.
The lies you rehearsed.
The moments you knew what was right but deliberately chose what was wrong.
And imagine that there is no way to defend yourself.
Because there isn't.
Romans 3:23 says all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
Not just the scandalous.
Not just the publicly disgraced.
Not just the people whose failures became gossip.
All.
The respectable sinner needs Jesus just as desperately as the publicly broken sinner.
The person who grew up in church needs grace.
The person who wasted years in rebellion needs grace.
The person who has never committed a notorious public sin still needs grace.
And the person who feels too ashamed to pray needs grace.
Now hear the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not die because humanity was already pure.
He died because we were not.
Romans 5:8 declares that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
That is the scandal of grace.
The Holy One gave Himself for the unholy.
The Righteous One died for the unrighteous.
The Sinless Savior bore the judgment sinners deserved.
And He rose from the dead, victorious over sin and death.
The cross is not God pretending sin does not matter.
The cross is the clearest demonstration of how seriously sin matters—and how deeply God loves sinners.
But there is another story you need to remember.
A woman was brought before Jesus in John 8.
Her accusers wanted judgment.
Her shame was public.
Her future seemed to be in the hands of people who were more interested in using her as a trap than restoring her life.
And Jesus refused to join their hypocrisy.
When her accusers departed, He told her:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more."
— John 8:11, KJV

There is an important textual note here: the account of the woman caught in adultery, John 7:53–8:11, is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts, and its original location in John's Gospel is disputed. The passage has nevertheless been received and treasured in much of the Christian tradition. Its portrayal of mercy joined with a call to holiness is consistent with teachings firmly established elsewhere in Scripture.
And notice those two truths.
"Neither do I condemn thee."
"Go, and sin no more."
Mercy.
And transformation.
Forgiveness.
And repentance.
Jesus does not offer a love that requires us to pretend our sins were righteous.
He offers a love that calls us away from sin and into new life.
And maybe that is exactly where this article has found you.
Perhaps you have been using grace as a reason to delay repentance.
You keep saying, "God understands."
And yes, He understands every weakness.
But He also knows the secret compromise you keep protecting.
Perhaps you have been living in a relationship you know dishonors Christ.
Perhaps pornography has become your private refuge.
Perhaps you have been nurturing an affair in your imagination long before anything happened physically.
Perhaps your pride has made you cruel to the people who love you.
Or perhaps your struggle is the opposite.
You have repented.
You have confessed.
You have turned away.
Yet you keep dragging yesterday's guilt into every new morning.
You believe Jesus forgives other people.
But somewhere deep inside, you suspect your own story is too damaged.
Listen to what the apostle John wrote:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
— 1 John 1:9, KJV
All unrighteousness.
Not only the sins that seem socially acceptable.
Not only the sins you can explain away.
Not only the failures that other Christians are comfortable hearing about.
All unrighteousness.
That promise belongs to those who come honestly to God through Jesus Christ.
And it does not mean that earthly consequences always disappear.
Trust may need rebuilding.
Relationships may require difficult conversations.
Wounds may take time to heal.
Some wrongs demand restitution.
Forgiveness does not magically undo every consequence of sin.
But the Gospel announces that guilt does not have to remain your master.
You can repent.
You can turn to Christ.
You can receive forgiveness.
And by the grace of God, you can begin walking differently.
That is why Revelation 19:7–8 gives us such a breathtaking picture of the final celebration of Christ and His people.
The marriage of the Lamb has come.
His wife has made herself ready.
And she is granted fine linen, clean and bright.
The passage identifies the fine linen with the righteous deeds of the saints, showing that the bride's preparation includes the holy lives of God's redeemed people.
Notice the balance.
She is granted her clothing.
And she is called to readiness.
God's grace does not eliminate the believer's response.
It makes faithful obedience possible.
The Church is not preparing herself through self-salvation.
She is responding to the redeeming work of the Lamb.
And one day, the people Christ has cleansed will stand before Him in the fullness of His saving work.
Not because their history was flawless.
But because their Savior is faithful.
Now return with me to Leviticus.
To that ancient command.
To the high priest who was required to marry a virgin from his people.
The immediate reason was the holiness and distinctiveness of the high priestly office and his household under Israel's covenant law.
That is what the passage actually teaches.
But when we read it within the completed witness of Scripture, we also encounter a greater story.
The old priesthood could not permanently remove sin.
Jesus can.
The old high priest had to offer sacrifices for his own sins.
Jesus had none.
The old system required repeated offerings.
Jesus offered Himself once for all.
And the Church, described as the bride of Christ, is being cleansed and sanctified by the very One who loves her.
We must not force Leviticus 21 to say everything the New Testament says about Christ.
But we should never read the Old Testament as though Jesus never came.
Because He did.
And His coming changes everything.
Perhaps the most astonishing part of this entire story is that Jesus did not wait for us to become worthy before loving us.
He loved us in our need.
He called us to repentance.
He bore our sins.
He rose again.
And He now calls us to belong wholly to Him.
Not halfway.
Not only on Sundays.
Not only when life is falling apart.
Wholly.
And this is where the question stops being merely historical.
Because the most important question is no longer simply, "Why was the high priest commanded to marry a virgin?"
The question becomes:
If Jesus has given Himself to make His people holy, why am I still clinging to the very sin He died to save me from?
That is not a question meant to crush the repentant.
It is a question meant to awaken the complacent.
If you are hiding sin, come into the light.
If you are exhausted from pretending, tell the truth.
If you are ashamed of your past, bring it to the Savior.
If you have wounded someone, pursue repentance and make things right where possible.
If you have been harmed by someone else's sin, understand this clearly: another person's wrongdoing does not make you spiritually contaminated or less worthy of dignity and care.
And if you have never surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, do not confuse familiarity with Christianity for saving faith.
Knowing Bible stories is not the same as knowing the Savior.
Admiring Jesus is not the same as trusting Him.
Religious activity cannot replace repentance and faith.
Today, you can turn to Him.
Not with a polished religious performance.
But with an honest heart.
"Lord Jesus, I have sinned. I cannot cleanse myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Forgive me. Turn my heart away from sin. Teach me to follow You. Make my life Yours."
There is no magic in the wording of a prayer.
Salvation rests in Jesus Christ, not in a formula.
But a heart that turns to Him in repentance and faith does not turn toward an unwilling Savior.
John 6:37 records His promise:
"Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out."
Let those words settle somewhere deeper than your shame.
"I will in no wise cast out."
And if this truth has touched something you have been carrying silently, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
You do not need to reveal private details or expose another person's story.
Sometimes a simple, honest response becomes the beginning of a conversation, a prayer, or the encouragement another struggling believer needs.
And if you have a testimony of how Jesus brought you from shame into repentance, forgiveness, and restoration, share what you are comfortable sharing.
Someone reading these words may be closer to giving up than you realize.
Your testimony might remind them that Christ is still able to save.
And please do not let this message stop with you.
Not merely because it deserves attention.
But because someone in your circle may have misunderstood God's holiness as hatred, or mistaken God's grace for permission to remain in sin.
Someone needs to understand both.
Send this to a family member who needs encouragement to return to Christ.
And invite even the person who does not yet believe to read the Gospel for themselves.
You never know which conversation God may use to open a heart.
Return to Leviticus 21, Hebrews 7–10, 1 Corinthians 6, Ephesians 5, and Revelation 19.
Read them in context.
Test what you hear against the Scriptures.
Let the Word of God—not merely an emotional moment—shape your understanding of holiness, repentance, marriage, forgiveness, and redemption.
It is about following the perfect Savior.
There is also something important I want to share with those who believe in this mission.

Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim Jesus Christ, strengthen believers, encourage repentance, help wounded hearts find biblical hope, and make discipleship resources more accessible to people who are hungry for God's Word.
That work requires time, dedication, resources, and faithful support.
He will not.
Not because you can purchase His favor.
You cannot.
It is neither.
But because the Gospel is worth proclaiming, biblical truth is worth defending, and discipleship is worth supporting.
There is an important biblical distinction here.
The New Testament teaches generosity that is willing rather than pressured.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 declares:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
That is the spirit in which I am inviting you.
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Joyfully.
And with a clear conscience before God.
You are not buying a blessing.
These products are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
But they can serve as reminders of biblical truth, encouragement in everyday life, and practical ways to support the continuing work of the ministry.
These free resources are part of our desire to make spiritual nourishment available beyond those who are able to contribute financially.
Because access to God's Word should never be confused with the purchase of God's grace.
Encourage someone who is struggling to return to Scripture.
Pray for the people who will encounter these messages.
And continue supporting the faithful work of your local church.
Because the goal is not to build an audience that simply admires religious content.
The goal is to point people to Jesus Christ.
To see sinners repent.
To see the weary strengthened.
To see the wounded cared for.
To see believers grow in truth.
To see people who once lived far from God discover the mercy of the crucified and risen Savior.
And perhaps that is the most important thing to remember about this entire passage.
The high priest's marriage requirement was never permission to despise those with complicated histories.
It was part of God's holy order for Israel's priesthood.
But that priesthood was not the final answer to humanity's sin.
Jesus Christ is.
He is the greater High Priest.
He is the sinless Savior.
He is the Bridegroom who gave Himself for His Church.
And He is coming again.
So do not let your past become an excuse to run from Him.
Do not let religious pride convince you that you never needed cleansing.
Do not let cheap grace persuade you that repentance is optional.
And do not let shame tell you that Christ's mercy is too small for a sinner who comes to Him.
The same Jesus who calls you to holiness is the Savior who gave Himself to make you holy.
That is why the Gospel is not a story about damaged people successfully disguising their brokenness.
It is the story of a holy Redeemer who saves sinners and transforms them by His grace.
Your past may explain where you have been, but it does not have the authority to overrule what Jesus Christ can do with a surrendered life.
